provenance: Original fictional teaching examples. No customer layouts, recipes, production traces or measured performance.

lessons.title: The material is here. Can we use it?
lessons.question: How do you keep the order moving when eligible material is short?
lessons.situation: The next order is due on line A. The warehouse has material, the team is ready, and the schedule says start. But physical stock and eligible stock are different things.
lessons.reference: Planning allocates an eligible lot. Warehouse confirms identity and quantity. Preparation verifies the addition before execution. Each handover carries a material identity and an accountable owner.
lessons.disruption: The allocated lot cannot cover the order. A similar material is nearby, but it is not approved for this product. Starting now could turn a scheduling problem into a product disposition problem.
lessons.owner: The planner coordinates; quality owns substitution eligibility; operations confirms line readiness.
lessons.assumption: Fictional discrete order. No real recipe, inventory quantity, duration or physical machine behaviour.
lessons.referenceState: Eligible lot allocated → verified addition → authorised execution.
lessons.currentState: Insufficient eligible material → preparation blocked → line start waits; packing needs a revised commitment.
evidence: Material identity, eligible quantity and allocation revision
Approved substitution criteria if an alternative is proposed
Revised sequence and acceptance of the changed commitment
prompts: Who may change the sequence, and who may approve a substitute?
Which event reports the shortage without authorising a workaround?
Who must know before the changed plan is executable?
lessons.facilitator: Distinguish “we have it” from “we may use it”. Invite a fourth response, then require its owner, evidence and consequences.

choices.title: Resequence eligible work
choices.action: Propose another eligible order; verify setup and readiness before starting.
choices.authority: Planner changes sequence; operations confirms readiness.
choices.material: The short order remains unconsumed; another eligible lot can be allocated.
choices.information: Publish revised sequence, order identity and delivery commitment.
choices.people: Warehouse, line and packing teams coordinate the changed handover.
choices.risk: Another order may need a changeover and delay the original commitment.

choices.title: Request an authorised substitute
choices.action: Hold the start while quality evaluates the alternative against approved criteria.
choices.authority: Quality authorises eligibility; planning and operations agree the executable plan.
choices.material: Keep the alternative segregated until approved and preserve its identity.
choices.information: Retain approval basis and revised allocation before release to execution.
choices.people: Quality needs evidence and time; the operator cannot approve by appearance.
choices.risk: Approval can be refused or arrive too late. This branch assumes a valid review process exists.

choices.title: Use the nearby material anyway
choices.action: Treat similar material as equivalent without an eligibility decision.
choices.authority: The line team has no substitution authority in this lesson.
choices.material: Unapproved input may require hold and assessment of affected output.
choices.information: A completion event would conceal an unresolved eligibility gap.
choices.people: Quality must investigate the affected scope.
choices.risk: Unacceptable shortcut: similarity is not evidence of suitability. Do not infer release.

lessons.title: Finished does not mean released.
lessons.question: What happens when a quality hold arrives after processing?
lessons.situation: Processing is complete and packing expects the lot. An outstanding result still determines whether it can proceed.
lessons.reference: Completion produces a traceable lot. Quality evaluates the evidence and records a disposition. Packing acts on the permitted state, not completion alone.
lessons.disruption: A result needs investigation. Quality holds the lot while scope and disposition are reviewed. Packing has already prepared for it.
lessons.owner: Quality owns disposition; operations preserves segregation; planning revises commitments.
lessons.assumption: Fictional hold with no actual test limits or product specification. No automated release.
lessons.referenceState: Process complete → evidence reviewed → authorised release → packing.
lessons.currentState: Process complete → hold active → packing eligibility blocked; investigation open.
evidence: Authorised disposition and evidence that affected consumers received it
prompts: Which physical movements remain permitted on hold?
How would you find a consumer that missed the hold event?
What evidence closes the hold rather than hiding it?
lessons.facilitator: Ask who means machine completion, order completion or product release when they say “finished”.

choices.title: Segregate and replan
choices.action: Preserve lot identity in controlled hold storage and revise packing sequence.
choices.authority: Quality retains disposition; operations manages permitted movement.
choices.material: Held stock stays identifiable and separate from releasable stock.
choices.information: Hold scope reaches packing, stock and planning; receipt needs evidence.
choices.people: Packing considers other work while quality investigates.
choices.risk: The hold may expand; revised packing may introduce additional setup.

choices.title: Release on machine completion
choices.action: Use machine completion as permission to pack and dispatch.
choices.authority: Equipment completion grants no quality-release authority.
choices.material: Held product may lose segregation and reach dispatch.
choices.information: A valid event is incorrectly interpreted as disposition.
choices.people: Operators inherit a decision they are not authorised to make.
choices.risk: Unacceptable shortcut: release is unsupported and affected output needs containment.

lessons.title: The next order needs a different line.
lessons.question: Which readiness conditions must survive a changeover?
lessons.situation: The next order uses a different format. Planning sees available time; the line still carries the previous setup and identifiers.
lessons.reference: Confirm sequence, clear previous material and labels, complete setup, verify first output and authorise the start under the local procedure.
lessons.disruption: A required setup part is unavailable. The planned start is not feasible, and labels from the previous order remain at the station.
lessons.owner: Operations owns readiness; maintenance verifies setup; quality owns required first-output disposition.
lessons.assumption: Illustrative readiness gates. No cleaning validation, safety procedure or measured changeover duration.
lessons.currentState: Missing setup part and unresolved clearance → next-order start blocked.
evidence: Line-clearance record including remaining labels and material
Verified configuration and availability of required parts
First-output verification and authorised readiness decision
prompts: Does a released schedule prove readiness?
Who can approve a changed setup?
What makes the first unit traceable to the correct configuration?
lessons.facilitator: Ask which readiness evidence this operation requires; avoid presenting a universal checklist.

choices.title: Complete readiness before starting
choices.action: Delay the start, obtain the correct part and complete clearance and verification.
choices.authority: Operations coordinates; maintenance and quality confirm their gates.
choices.material: Separate previous material and avoid premature consumption.
choices.information: Publish revised readiness and schedule; retain configuration history.
choices.people: Planning communicates delay while the line team closes outstanding conditions.
choices.risk: The commitment moves; waiting does not itself solve the missing part.

choices.title: Start and verify later
choices.action: Begin the next order with incomplete setup and clearance.
choices.authority: Schedule pressure does not waive readiness gates.
choices.material: Incorrect format or mixed identifiers may affect output.
choices.information: The order appears running while readiness remains unproven.
choices.people: The team absorbs unapproved risk and may need to contain output.
choices.risk: Unacceptable shortcut: later inspection cannot be assumed to repair lost identity.

lessons.title: The scanner is down. The boundary stays.
lessons.question: What makes a workaround controlled rather than convenient?
lessons.situation: Preparation normally verifies material by scanning. The scanner is unavailable, but material and order are present.
lessons.reference: Verify material against the authorised order and record identity, quantity and accountable handover before addition.
lessons.disruption: The normal identity check cannot be recorded. Verbal confirmation would keep work moving but removes expected evidence.
lessons.owner: Operations authorises a temporary procedure within its mandate; quality defines identity evidence and restrictions.
lessons.assumption: The controlled branch assumes a reviewed manual fallback procedure exists. Without one, that branch is unavailable in a real operation.
lessons.referenceState: Identity verified and recorded → authorised addition.
lessons.currentState: Verification unavailable → addition blocked; temporary procedure not yet activated.
evidence: Approved temporary procedure, scope, owner and expiry
Reconciliation against the order and confirmation of restored normal operation
prompts: Who authorises the fallback, for which orders and until when?
What prevents the workaround becoming permanent?
lessons.facilitator: Ask what makes the controlled branch unavailable. “No approved fallback” is a valid reason to stop.

choices.title: Activate the approved fallback
choices.action: Authorise the scoped procedure, independently verify identity and retain reconciliation records.
choices.authority: The procedure owner authorises scope and expiry; operators perform its checks.
choices.material: Material remains blocked until the required identity checks are complete.
choices.information: Record degraded mode, verification evidence and later reconciliation.
choices.people: Assign checking and restoration responsibilities explicitly.
choices.risk: Manual checks add effort and error exposure; the fallback cannot waive eligibility rules.

choices.title: Stop until verification is restored
choices.action: Hold the addition and restore normal verification.
choices.authority: Operations protects the gate and escalates the delivery impact.
choices.material: No unverified addition; material identity remains intact.
choices.information: Expose the blocked state and revised commitment.
choices.people: Support restores verification; planning manages delay.
choices.risk: Production waits; restoration timing is unknown.

choices.title: Take a verbal confirmation
choices.action: Proceed without the required procedure and retained evidence.
choices.authority: Verbal assurance does not establish approval or a record.
choices.material: An unverified addition may make genealogy uncertain.
choices.information: No reliable record remains to reconcile after restoration.
choices.people: Responsibility becomes ambiguous and investigation harder.
choices.risk: Unacceptable shortcut: the missing check is concealed rather than controlled.
